newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat sorry at Israeli deaths; angry over talks.
newsitem.headline: Arafat sorry at Israeli deaths; angry over talks.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, in remarks broadcast on Friday, expressed sorrow at the killing of seven Israeli schoolgirls by a Jordanian soldier and said the most important thing now was to push peace forward.

Asked by Israel Radio if he would meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Palestinian president said in English: "I have no objection. The most important thing (is) how to push forward the peace process".

"I am very sorry at what had happened and I contacted his excellency the president and his excellency the prime minister and offered my condolences by the name of the Palestinian people," Arafat said. Arafat was speaking late on Thursday.
The telephone call to Netanyahu was the first contact between the two leaders since Arafat last week angrily rejected a planned Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank.

In an interview published on Friday in Israel's mass circulation Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper Arafat said PLO-Israel relations were in the deepest crisis since their 1993 Oslo peace accords. The interview was given before Thursday's shooting.

"This is not just 'another crisis,'" he said. "This is the most serious crisis since the Oslo process began, and it has far-reaching implications. You can say the process has stopped. The government of Israel has stopped it."

The crisis was triggered by two Israeli decisions: a plan to build 6,500 more homes for Jews on land captured in 1967 between East Jerusalem and Bethlehem and a decision that the first of three scheduled Israeli pullbacks from the West Bank would be only a third of the size demanded by the PLO.

"The government of Israel is simply misleading us," Arafat told Yedioth. "It's decisions that it wants to impose on us are literally a conspiracy against peace. And Israel is the one that will bear all the results of that."
The interviewer noted that Israel contends the decisions did not contradict peace accords.

"They contradict the letter and the spirit of the accords," Arafat replied. "The fact is the whole world thinks so, and said so at the United Nations. Is the whole world wrong and only Netanyahu right?"
The U.N. General Assembly voted 130 to 2 on Thursday to call on Israel to abandon the Jerusalem settlement plan. The United States and Israel cast the only votes against the resolution.
Israel on Friday rejected the General Assembly resolution and said construction would begin next week.
Arafat attacked the U.S. veto, noting that American officials also had expressed concern over the Israeli plan.

"I don't understand this crooked dialectic: they vote against what they think is right. They are with us in objecting to the Israeli plans. Just the head forgot to give an order to the hand how to vote. Their veto is serious and has dangerous implications for the whole region."
Arafat rejected the idea Netanyahu was subject to pressures from right-wing members of his government.

"That's strange. He has to be pressed? After all, he agrees with them," Arafat was quoted as saying. "If he wants to lead Israel into an era of peace he has to reject the pressures, if they are real. But we believe he is of one mind with the extremists and only when he really has no choice he corrects the course a little."
